text: What would you write down, if your city was on fire?
London, sixteen sixty-six. Samuel Pepys keeps a secret diary, in a private shorthand. Almost every day, for nine years, he writes down his life.
At three in the morning, on the second of September, his maid wakes him. There's a fire, in Pudding Lane. He looks out of the window, decides it's far away, and goes back to bed.
But by morning, it isn't far away at all. Hundreds of houses have already burned.
So Pepys climbs the Tower of London, to see it for himself. He takes a boat along the river. Then he tells the King the only way to stop it: pull houses down.
That night, he carries his belongings into the garden, by moonlight. Days later, he buries his wine, and his Parmesan cheese, in a pit.

In the end, over thirteen thousand houses, eighty-seven churches, and Saint Paul's Cathedral are lost. But Pepys had sent his diary to safety. And because he wrote it all down, we can stand in that room today.
The diary sat almost unread, for years. Then a student spent three years cracking the shorthand. It was first published in eighteen twenty-five.
Pepys leaves us three habits. Write it the same day, while the details are fresh. Record the big and the small together. And keep your notebook safe.
Try a Pepys page, tonight. The time. The place. One thing someone said. One thing you carried. And one feeling, in plain words. Ten minutes is plenty.
